claims.claim: The lithograph print lists the giant's whole length as 10 feet 4½ inches
claims.quote: Whole length of the figure, 10 feet, 4½ inches

claims.claim: The lithograph print gives the length of the nose as six inches
claims.quote: length of nose, 6 inches

claims.claim: The lithograph is titled "The Onondaga Giant" and is credited to Popular Graphic Arts
claims.quote: Title:  The  Onondaga giant ... Author: Popular Graphic Arts

claims.claim: Two men dug the well in which the giant was found
claims.quote: Newell hired Gideon Emmons and Henry Nichols, ostensibly to dig a well, and on October 16, 1869, they found the giant

claims.claim: The diggers found the giant on 16 October 1869
claims.quote: on October 16, 1869, they found the giant

claims.claim: Cornell's president noted that good water already ran past the house
claims.quote: that there was already a good spring and a stream of water running conveniently to both

claims.claim: The giant photograph is a Bain News Service image dated 1910, public domain
claims.quote: Date: 1910 Author: Bain News Service, publisher Licence: Public domain

claims.claim: The stone for the giant came from a glen/quarry in Iowa
claims.quote: This is the Gypsum Quarry from which was taken the block out of which the original "Cardiff Giant" was carved.

claims.claim: Hull's men cut a roughly ten-foot gypsum block at Fort Dodge, Iowa, in 1868
claims.quote: In 1868, Hull, accompanied by a man named H. B. Martin, hired men to quarry out a 10-foot-4.5-inch-long (3.2 m) block of gypsum in Fort Dodge, Iowa

claims.claim: Hull told the quarrymen the block was intended for a Lincoln monument
claims.quote: telling them it was intended for a monument to Abraham Lincoln in New York

claims.claim: The stereocard view is of Cardiff Glen, Fort Dodge, Iowa, dated 1873, scanned by NYPL
claims.quote: View in Cardiff Glen, near Fort Dodge, Iowa. Date: 1873 Author: Scan by NYPL

claims.claim: Hull confessed in 1869
claims.quote: On December 10, 1869, Hull confessed everything to the press

claims.claim: The Cardiff Giant is still on display
claims.quote: In 1947, he sold it to the Fenimore Farm & Country Village in Cooperstown, New York, where it is still displayed.

claims.claim: The reverse of the stereocard names George Hull and H. B. Martin as the perpetrators
claims.quote: Their names were George Hull and H. B. Martin.

claims.claim: It is unclear whether the Chicago stonecutter knew what he was carving
claims.quote: While it is not clear if Burkhardt was aware of Hull's intentions

claims.claim: The Cardiff Giant was not a real petrified man; it was gypsum carved to order
claims.quote: The Cardiff Giant was one of the most famous archaeological hoaxes in American history.

claims.claim: George Hull was a New York tobacconist
claims.quote: The giant was the creation of a New York tobacconist named George Hull.

claims.claim: The block went to a Chicago stonecutter
claims.quote: He shipped the block to Edward Burkhardt in Chicago, a German stonecutter.

claims.claim: Two sculptors carved the ten-foot figure, modelled on Hull himself
claims.quote: Burkhardt hired two sculptors named Henry Salle and Fred Mohrmann to create the giant. ... The giant was designed to imitate the form of Hull himself.

claims.claim: A geologist told Hull hair would not petrify, so the figure has none
claims.quote: Hull consulted a geologist and learned that hairs would not be petrified, so he removed the hair and beard from the giant.

claims.claim: The surface was beaten with steel knitting needles embedded in a board to simulate pores
claims.quote: The giant's surface was beaten with steel knitting needles embedded in a board to simulate pores.

claims.claim: The figure was rubbed with sulphuric acid to make it look older
claims.quote: The giant was also rubbed with sulphuric acid to create a deeper, vintage-like color.

claims.claim: It was buried on his cousin William Newell's farm in late November 1868
claims.quote: On a night in late November 1868, the giant was buried in a hole in Newell's farm.

claims.claim: Newell charged fifty cents for a fifteen-minute viewing
claims.quote: a tent was set up on the discovery site and Newell charged each visitor fifty cents for a fifteen-minute session of viewing the giant

claims.claim: Three to five hundred visitors came per day
claims.quote: The number of visitors went to about three to five hundred per day

claims.claim: Andrew D. White was Cornell's first president and saw no reason to dig a well at that spot
claims.quote: Andrew D. White, the first president of Cornell University, made a close inspection of the Cardiff Giant. He noticed that there was no good reason to try to dig a well in the exact spot the giant had been found.

claims.claim: Yale's O. C. Marsh called the giant "a most decided humbug", noting soluble gypsum with fresh tool marks
claims.quote: Yale paleontologist Othniel C. Marsh examined the statue, pointing out that it was made of soluble gypsum, which, had it been buried in its blanket of wet earth for centuries, would not still have fresh tool marks on it (which it did), and termed it "a most decided humbug".

claims.claim: Hull confessed on 10 December 1869 and said he had always meant the hoax to be exposed
claims.quote: On December 10, 1869, Hull confessed everything to the press ... but confessed proudly that he intended for the hoax to be exposed

claims.claim: On 2 February 1870 a court declared both the giant and Barnum's plaster copy fakes
claims.quote: on February 2, 1870, both giants were revealed as fakes in court

claims.claim: Barnum's copy was a plaster copy modelled covertly in wax
claims.quote: he hired a man to model the giant's shape covertly in wax and create a plaster copy

claims.claim: The copy in a Michigan arcade is said to be Barnum's on the word of the arcade's owner
claims.quote: The owner of Marvin's Marvelous Mechanical Museum, a coin-operated game arcade and museum of oddities in Farmington Hills, Michigan, has said that the copy displayed there is Barnum's.

claims.claim: The lithograph dates from 1869
claims.quote: Entered according to Act of Congress, in the year 1869, by A. L. Edwards, in the Clerk's Office, of the District Court, for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania.
